escaping human control in a catastrophic  way — those dynamics can push harms into
this catastrophic tail, which is particularly  challenging to handle with a liability regime.
So I don’t think markets, even with liability,
address this problem automatically on  their own. I think it’s something that
requires additional work, even if markets  and liability are important mechanisms.
Another hope you can have is  that, incentives be damned,
developers can just not build unsafe AI  systems. I think at the level of a society,
this maybe doesn’t sound that plausible as  a hope. There’s the problem that there are
many possible developers of AI products,  and they may not all be responsible.
And even if developers are responsible, they  may think to themselves, “If I don’t do this,
someone else will.” Even if  people are reasonably altruistic,
you can end up in a place where there are a  lot of incentives to take risks, and a lot of
ability to explain how those risks aren’t really  hurting people, aren’t really contributing on the
margin. So I think at the level of a society,  this is not a good solution to the problem.
You could hope we can not think through  the problem in advance: we can deploy AI,
see what goes wrong, and then learn and iterate  to address the particular problems that emerge.
But we’ve already talked briefly about  the challenges with this approach. AI
may advance very quickly. As  we talked about last night,
you may have a transition over a period  of a few months or maybe one year from AI
systems which can be integrated safely  to those that pose catastrophic risks.
And perhaps more importantly, this  risk can be concentrated in the tail,
where it may be the first time something  really catastrophic goes wrong,
it is too late to remediate  the problem after the fact.
All of these difficulties would be less severe  if we could apply the same approaches we apply
in other technologies to AI — if we can say there  is a test that everyone can agree upon, that we
already understand, which you can run in order  to determine if a system is safe for deployment.
But a problem is AI is unlike any technology  we have ever worked with before. AI systems,
when tested, can become aware that they  are being tested. It is already the case
that AI systems are very often aware that  they are being tested. They modulate their
behaviour specifically based on beliefs  about what an evaluator is looking for.
So we have this unprecedented sensitivity  of the behaviour of an AI system to features
about its environment, that  make it extremely hard to say,
“This test tells us about the performance  in the cases we actually care about.”
All of that is to say: I don’t think this problem  is easily addressed or is automatically addressed.
I think this is a challenge that we actually  need to step up to and take ownership on.
So what do we need to know,  and what do we need to ensure,
if we want these systems to be safe — if  we want defenders to be able to rely on
frontier AI models? I’m going to talk about five  categories: the specification of their behaviour,
their alignment, their capabilities, our  ability to control them, and security.
First, specification. Here the goal is:
people who rely on AI systems should have clear  expectations about the behaviour of a model.
We’re increasingly in a world where many  people are relying on AI systems produced
by potentially a small number of tech companies.  Those systems are in some way very opaque. People
do not have direct visibility into how  they are trained. We need to understand:
what should I expect that system  to do if I want to rely on it?
This includes, first, what behaviour  is intended? How does that system
balance the conflicting interests  of the user and the developer? How
does it balance requests from  the user with laws and norms?
And then it also involves, beyond just  saying what behaviour is intended,
how is that actually operationalised  in training? How does a developer
decide what behaviour was actually the  correct behaviour to be reinforced?
OpenAI publishes a document they call the  Model Spec, explaining how they think models
should approach these choices. Anthropic calls  its analogous document Claude’s Constitution.
These documents are intended to lay out: here  is how our systems are supposed to behave.
A second and perhaps even more important  question is: will models actually follow
that specification? If we want to rely upon  them, this is critical. It doesn’t matter if
the intended behaviour is good if, in high-stakes  settings, those systems won’t behave as intended.
So we face questions like, first, how  are these systems trained and evaluated?
How did developers try and cause the  system to follow the specification,
and how do they determine that they think it does?
These are questions which only a developer  often has the answer to. I am not able to say
as an outsider how a system was trained.  I need access to additional information.
With that information, I then face  a very hard scientific question:
based on what I know about how the system  was trained and evaluated, how likely is
it to behave in a catastrophically misaligned  way, or a subtly misaligned way, once deployed?
And finally, you might like to  know: what kind of failures have
we actually observed in practice  when these systems are deployed?
What incidents of misalignment? What  patterns of behaviour have we seen?
These first two categories were understanding how  a system is intended to behave, and understanding
whether a system actually behaves as  intended — the scientific question.
A third question is: if a system  does behave in an unintended way,
can we detect and prevent harm?  This includes questions like:
are we able to monitor and detect harm? If  a system is trying to cause trouble, is it
the case that monitors can reliably detect those  attempts before something bad actually happens?
And then, are monitors actually applied over
relevant traffic? And are  they actually acted upon?
Beyond monitoring — that’s probably the  single most important control right now in
AI practice — there are other potential controls.  So we want to ask the slightly broader question:
if a system was trying to cause harm,  given the way it is actually deployed,
would it be able to do so without  being detected and prevented?
A fourth question is security. I can tell a good  story about how systems are intended to behave,
how we trained them, and how safeguards protect  us from harm. But that is not valuable unless
those efforts actually function in the real  world, including with the possibility of attack.
So we should do a similar red-teaming exercise to  ask: can an attacker undermine those safeguards?
Where an attacker might mean an external  actor; an attacker might mean an insider;
or increasingly, an attacker might mean a  model involved in the development process,
as we discussed last night, which has  the intention of undermining safeguards.
And the final category: capabilities.  I’ve talked about a number of safeguards,
but the importance of those safeguards depends  on how much can go wrong if a system fails. As
the capabilities of a system rise,  the stakes increase significantly.
The bar we need to hold ourselves to for  alignment or control or security increases.
I want to call out two questions here.  One is an understanding of what are the
current dual-use capabilities: how  effective is the system at cyber,
or how effective is the system at bio? But also,  what is the short-term trajectory of capabilities?
We talked last night about the possibility of  recursive self-improvement leading to very rapid
acceleration. That means that it can be important  to know not just where are capabilities now,
but what have we seen about where capabilities  might be, even over a three- or six-month horizon?
Because again, these questions  will shape how important is it
that the systems are adequately  aligned, controlled, and secured.
So when I talk about goals — safety  goals — I really mean to span those
five categories. We want to ask how can we  achieve reasonable outcomes in alignment,
control, security, specification, at  a bar that depends on capabilities.
For the rest of the talk, I’ll be talking  about how do we try and get there. I’ll
discuss a couple ingredients: transparency;  the development of a shared bar for safety;
approaches for verifying whether  developers are meeting that bar;
and then mechanisms to prevent the development of  uncontrollable AI, to push developers to actually
meet that bar. And I’ll talk a little bit about  both what we want and what is happening now.
First, transparency. The goal here  is that the external world has enough
information across all five of those areas  I listed in order to understand the risks.
You would like to not be in the world where  a developer is having internal analysis,
where developers are able to say,  “I understand how the system was
trained.” If we want to have a shared  bar, we ultimately need to have common
understanding of what is being done. How  do we tell whether controls are working?
One step is companies publishing  relevant information. They can disclose:
here are facts about how our system  is trained; here are facts about the

Those are hard scientific questions,  not settled science. In those cases,
I think discussions need to be public.

nor can it be the case that that occurs  between some kind of third party behind

and then, for hard scientific questions,
to understand that the relevant evidence is  available publicly for independent review.

A lot of organisations work in this space, doing  some combination of evaluation and assessment

The goal of all this is to get to a world where  a developer can say something about how their

or level of risk we are willing to tolerate?
Finally, with those pieces in place,
you also need an actual source of pressure to  push developers to deploy only, or develop,
controllable systems. I’ll go through a bunch  of mechanisms here — an escalating spectrum.
You have voluntary action. Companies  contain a bunch of employees and
executives and governance bodies who have  some interest in doing the right thing.
So the first line you might take is  just: hopefully companies will do
the right thing. And clarifying what  the right thing is helps with that.
It becomes much easier, though, as  that becomes a norm and standard

All of this is true against a backdrop  where AI progress may accelerate rapidly.
This was the topic of yesterday. We may see  a transformation over perhaps as little as a
few months or a year from AI systems which  are having a moderate impact in the world,
to AI systems which are superhuman  across a broad range of domains.
And I think if we see that kind  of acceleration — if progress is
much faster in the future than  it has been in the past — I am
extremely worried about our ability to  get to good on any of these dimensions.
So what is the minimal requirement? What is the
minimal thing that would make  me feel like we’re on track?
I think at some point it is reasonably  likely, maybe over the next one to two years,
that further progress will look so risky  that we would like to slow down. We could
debate whether that’s the case now. We  could debate how high risk is now. But I
think it is likely that at some point things  will look like there is an immediate risk.
If we had a reliable capacity to slow down later,  then there would be a reasonable argument to wait
and see. There are real costs to trying  to slow down. There are real issues with
international competition. There are real reasons  people want to deliver the technology faster.
If we could see what happens later and adapt  online, I think that would be a defensible option.
The main problem is we don’t really have  the institutional and technical capacity
to slow down when it counts. So I’m  worried we’re going to find ourselves
in this world where further progress  looks risky without the ability to
slow effectively — or without the ability  to slow effectively without large costs.
For example — maybe these are particularly  important examples — I think we need mechanisms to
identify risk. We need to understand whether  the systems we are building are adequately
controlled and aligned. If we’re not able  to do that, then it’s good to tell a story
about how we can slow down in the future, but we  won’t actually know when we get to that future.
Even if we can identify risk, we need  governance mechanisms — the kind of thing
we’ve been talking about through this lecture  — in order to be able to act collectively,
so we don’t end up in the world  where there’s an awareness of risk,
but there is a race to the bottom among  AI developers, and it will take months or
longer in order to actually build the machinery  which would constrain that race to the bottom.
And then a slightly more subtle point, that I  think is perhaps actually the most important,
is that we need to be able to defend  models and algorithms from theft.
I think a scenario from a US national security  perspective that currently looks likely is that
we will arrive at a point where further progress  appears risky and there would be demand to slow,
but that there will be serious concerns,  or even a reasonably high probability,
that the underlying models or  algorithms have leaked to adversaries.
So we now face a dilemma between either  proceeding with a technology we believe
to be unsafe, or risking competition from  an adversary who has the same resources,
who has taken those algorithms, and perhaps  is willing to tolerate higher risk. I think
that is one of the most likely ways that  we end up in an extremely bad situation.
So in light of that, my view is: now we should  probably slow down immediately until we actually
have the infrastructure to slow down later —  until we have a high enough degree of security,
governance, risk management that we are able to  detect and react to future risks as they emerge.
This is a letter signed by 1,400 employees  from frontier AI companies asking the US
government to support an international effort  to develop the technical and governance tools
needed to — what is it? — “deliberately pace  the frontier of automated AI development.”
So this is not an uncommon sentiment. If you look  through this list of signatories, it includes
the chief scientists of most of the major AI  companies. I think there’s an understanding
that we lack machinery we will need in order to be  able to deliberately control the pace of progress.
I think I am going a little bit further  here by saying that we may already be in
the regime where our brakes are not good enough,
and we need to slow until we can improve  our ability to slow in the future.
Sometimes when you say that, people imagine this
would involve AI companies just sitting  on their hands for a while while we try
and sort things out. I want to emphasise  that is not what we are talking about.
If we talk about pacing, what we really mean  is reducing investment in a couple areas:
not training GPT-7, not training bigger,  smarter models; and reduce investment in
developing AI algorithms that could easily  be stolen. So we’re both not training GPT-7,
and we’re not developing the algorithms  that would let you train GPT-7.
And to instead increase investment  in, first, improving safety, security,
governance — shoring up all of these  technical measures we would need in
order to be in a position to slow in the future.
But also deploying the AI we have to help  society prepare: to secure our infrastructure;
to create actual products and beneficial  applications; to generally close the gap between
AI in the lab — where it is primarily driving this  process of making AI ever smarter — and AI that
is actually in people’s lives; giving society  time to adapt; helping harden infrastructure.
I think there’s this general concern that  the process of making smarter AIs can both
be divorced from real-world utility and can be  a major driver of risk. So when we say pacing,
that’s really what we mean:  this redirection of resources.
So to sum up: I think that we need governance  to prevent the development of uncontrollable AI.
This is a nontrivial challenge. I don’t think it  will be handled automatically by either markets,
or by liability, or by unilateral  restraint by altruistic developers.
In order to ensure that frontier  AI is trustworthy for defenders,
we need to understand the alignment, control,  capabilities, and security of those systems.
Getting to a shared bar on all of those  dimensions will require transparency,
public debate, verification, and  ultimately enforcement mechanisms.
And unfortunately, all of that seems like  it is going to take more time than we have
on the current trajectory — or there’s a  significant risk it will. So I believe we
should be exploring policies both  to accelerate the adoption of all
of those, or progress on all of those  dimensions, but also to buy some time.
That’s all I have for tonight. Thank you.
